title: Jewel Mirror Samadhi Part 3
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart invites listeners to explore the idea that there are aspects of reality that cannot be grasped by our ordinary thinking and conceptual frameworks. Instead, they suggest experiencing these "naturally real" yet "inconceivable" concepts directly, allowing us to tap into their transformative power without analysis or interpretation. This approach requires a willingness to let go of our need for understanding and instead simply be present with the experience, embracing its complexity and uncertainty.

sentences.text: *Now you have it, so keep it well.
Filling a silver bowl with snow, hiding a heron in the moonlight.
Taken as similar, they are not the same.
When you mix them, you know where they are.
The meaning is not in the words, yet it responds to the inquiring impulse.
Move and you are trapped.
Miss and you fall into doubt and vacillation.
Turning away and touching are both wrong, for it is like a massive fire.
Just to depict it in literary form is to stain it with defilement.
It's bright just at midnight.
It doesn't appear at dawn.
It acts as a guide for beings.
Its use removes all pains.
Although it is not fabricated, it is not without speech.
It's like facing the jewel mirror.
Form an image, behold each other.
You are not it.
In truth it is you.*
*Like a babe in the world, in five aspects complete, it does not go or come, nor rise, nor stand.
Baba, baba, is there anything said or not?
Ultimately it does not apprehend anything because its speech is not yet correct.
It is like the six lines of the illumination hexagram.
Relative and ultimate interact.
Piled up they make three.
The complete transformation makes five.
It is like the taste of the five flavored herb.
Like a diamond thunderbolt, subtly included within the true, inquiry and response come up together.
Communing with the source, travel the pathways, embrace the territory and treasure the road.
Respecting this is fortunate, do not neglect it.
Yet inconceivable is it not within the province of delusion or enlightenment.*
*With causal conditions, time and season quiescently it shines bright.
In its fineness it fits into spacelessness.
In its greatness it is utterly beyond location.
A hair spread's deviation will fail to accord with the proper attunement.
Now there is sudden and gradual in which teachings and approaches arise.
Once basic approaches are distinguished, then there are guiding rules.
But even though the basis is reached and the approach comprehended, true eternity still flows.
Outwardly still, while inwardly moving, like a tethered coal, the trapped rat.
The ancient sages pitied them and bestowed upon them the teaching.*
*According to their delusions, they call black as white.
When erroneous imagination sees, the acquiescent mind realizes itself.
If you want to conform to the ancient way, please observe the sages' former times.
When about to fulfill the way of Buddhahood, one gazed at a tree for ten eons.
Like a battle-scarred tiger, like a horse with shanks gone gray.
Because there is the common there, jeweled pedestals, fine clothing.
Because there is the startlingly different there, house cat and cow.
Yi with his archer skill could hit a target at a hundred paces, arrow points meet head-on.*
*What has this to do with the power of skill?
When the wooden man begins to sing, the stone woman gets up dancing.
It's not within reach of feeling or discrimination.
How could it admit of consideration and thought?
Ministers serve their lords, children obey their parents.
Not obeying is not filial, and not serving is no help.
Practice secretly, working within, like a fool, like an idiot.
Just to continue in this way is called the host within the host.*
Good evening, my friends.
Thanks for being so nice to me that you come to these talks.
Because if you didn't come, I wouldn't have reason to write them.
And it makes me very happy to sit at home and totally geek out.
I'm really trying to restrain myself in this series to not analyze it to the max, because that would be supremely unhelpful.
This text is something to be experienced, something to dance with.
Not something to say, "Oh, this means this, and that means that, and A plus B is C, and 1 plus 2 is 3."
So I'm really challenging you to feel into this text, and to humor me when I bring in things that are seemingly or rightfully totally unrelated.
The first passage I want to tackle, and feel free to look at it in the book, too:
*Naturally real, yet inconceivable.
It is not within the province of delusion or enlightenment.
With causal conditions, time and season, quiescently it shines bright.
In its fineness, it fits into spacelessness.
In its greatness, it is utterly beyond location.*
What really grabbed me is that first sentence: *naturally real, yet inconceivable.
It is not within the province of delusion or enlightenment.* There's something in there that just pulls the carpet out from under us.
We tend to organize our experience very quickly.
This is clear, that is confused.
This is working, that doesn't work for me.
And this just totally removes that frame.
Not within the province of delusion or enlightenment.
If you take those two things away, what is left?
If it's not enlightenment, if it's not ultimate reality, if it's not delusion, where can you find a place to stand?
It doesn't allow us to evaluate ourselves the way we usually do.
Naturally real means it's already so, and at the same time inconceivable.
Not something we can get a hold of or pin down.
And yet, if we allow ourselves to wonder, there are inconceivable things in our life.
Looking up at the night sky, seeing those incredible images from the Hubble telescope, can we really truly conceive of stars being born in cosmic dust?
Can we really conceive that the iron in our bodies comes from the explosions of dying suns?
Can we really believe that a part of us already crossed interstellar space and that it is allowing us to breathe, to absorb oxygen?
How inconceivable is that?
So things arise when the conditions are there.
No dying suns, no oxygen-binding iron.
Things arise when the conditions are there, and we can trust that.
Not because we are perfect, not because we have forced something into being, but because causes and conditions have come together.
And when they do, it shines bright, quietly.
Not as something dramatic or special, but just as this moment of functioning.
In its fineness, it does fit into spacelessness, and in its greatness it is utterly beyond location.
There is something very intimate here, very small, right in front of us and within us, and at the same time not confined.
You can see how the text did successfully remove any landing pad for us.

Now I'm going to shift into the next section, and I want to do something a little different this time, because I'm not going to talk about any meaning in this passage, but listen how often the number five pops up.
*As a babe in the world in five aspects complete, it does not go or come, nor rise nor stand.
Ba ba ba ba, is there anything said or not?
Ultimately it does not apprehend anything, because its speech is not yet correct.
It is like the six lines of the illumination hexagram.
Relative and ultimate interact.
Piled up, they make three.
The complete transformation makes five.
It is like the taste of the five-flavored herb, like a diamond [unclear: "from the mold"].*
And that also has five corners.
So there's a lot of fives here: in five aspects complete, the complete transformation makes five, the five-flavored herb.
There is this thing called the five ranks, also known as Dongshan's five ranks.
And Mari is going to hand out a few pages.
Sorry, my printer died.
It ran out of ink and I didn't have any more at home.
You won't really need it.
I will bring more copies next week when we have our last session on this.
Dongshan, when we talked about who he was last time and the time before, came up with a model of how we can see ourselves in practice.
The first is called the apparent within the real, and that is called the host.
It's symbolized as a black dot with a little white space in it.
It symbolizes that we carry a lot of conditioning within us, but we've gotten a glimpse of the absolute.
That is the apparent within the real.
The next image is the real within the apparent, and it's symbolized by this white space with a black dot in it.
That one is the guest.
That means you have a pretty good grasp on your Dharma practice, and you do know that there is a space that you still need to work with for a bit.
And that space is shrinking in the third position, which is coming from within the real, which is basically white with just a tiny, tiny black dot.
Then the next position is called the guest returning to host, which is all white.
In our heart of hearts, we would really, really like to get there, to this place of enlightenment, where we can tell everybody, "I finally got it.
I know what the Buddha saw when he saw the morning star."
In our conventional thinking, that is the most desirable.
Well, surprise, surprise.
There is a fifth position, which is the same circle, and it's all blacked out.
And we go, "No, I don't want this.
I want to really get it and stay there.
I want to live there forever."
But we need to see reality.
We need to see ourselves just the way we are.
We need to see our delusions and understand that those delusions are a piece of right now, just the way we are.
This is who we are.
If we wait until we are all the white bubble and the shining light, and we think that that's it, we are misled.
Remember in the ox herding pictures, the last one is to return to the marketplace.
The last step is we need to re-enter this society that we have, and we need to take care of it.
We need to take very good care of it, because this wonderful life that we have, it's easy to lose it.
There are many poetic and visual ways that point out the relative and the absolute and how they interplay and interact, and they are not separate.
They are always interacting.
At one moment I might feel like there is a really solid me here, and then I see there isn't.
Things feel separate, sometimes difficult, something to manage.
In another moment something shifts and functioning just happens: speaking, moving, responding without the same tight sense of a center of a me.
And then it shifts again.
So the five ranks are not steps to climb.
They are not a ladder where you say, "Oh, I finally got it, I made it all the way to the top."
They are more like different ways experience shows up, different ways this interaction of relative and ultimate can be lived.
Sometimes they feel distinct, sometimes they blur into each other.
Sometimes they all seem to be present at once in ways that are impossible to name.
The five ranks try to show that movement.
Black and white are never fixed, and they are not separate territories.
They flow into each other, and the poem that we read the first two sessions, Dumoulin's translation of Dongshan's five ranks, is just another way of expressing this.
It's not a system we master, but something we live into, something we resonate with, something to dance with.
Even if you stumble, it's still a dance.
If you're interested, take some time with it at home.
There is no way to get it.
Sometimes I even have the delusion that I understand some of this, and then I look at it again and go, "Nah."
It's like that baby in the text.
Is there anything said or not?
Not yet correct, not yet able to say it, and it's still complete, because that's what babies say.
Now the third section that I want to talk about tonight:
*Outwardly still, while inwardly moving, like a tethered colt, like a trapped rat, the ancient sages pitied them and bestowed upon them the teaching.*
I think a lot of us know about these states.
Outwardly still, everything looks fine.
Someone looks at us in meditation and says, "Oh, they must have got it.
They look so peaceful."
And the mind of that person might just churn like crazy.
Agitation, planning, being lost in thought, sometimes nothing at all.
Just frozen, not able to move forward, not able to step back, just caught.
It can be anything, something small and ordinary: a conversation we do not know how to enter, a decision we cannot make, a job we are avoiding like heck, something I cannot let go of.
Outwardly still, inwardly moving, just frozen.
I told you a week ago that one of my gecko babies was hatching.
And that actually reminds me of that state: just the nose and two little paws are looking out.
You don't know, can it break free of the shell?
Is it going to live?
Is it going to die?
Is it going to hatch and get eaten by mom right away?
It happens all the time.
So the little baby was not fully there, not fully out, but not in any longer.
Already alive, but not what we call complete.
There is a kind of in-between there, a kind of stuckness that is not wrong.
It's just the way it is at that moment.
Another translation is a mouse frozen by fright.

And that can describe a practitioner who is actually quite advanced, a practitioner who has reached a level where they exist rather contentedly and peacefully, but they are frozen by fright because they know if they go in deeper, they're going to lose that peace, at least for a while.
That is a mouse frozen by fright.
The text says that the ancient sages pitied them and bestowed upon them the teaching.
I do not hear that as judgment.
I hear that as compassion.
This condition we might find ourselves in, stuck, unsure, frozen, is not a personal failure.
That is what it means to be human.
And the teaching is given right there, not somewhere else, not when we finally get it.
It's right here, and not to fix ourselves, but right in the middle of it.
So I want to read you another poem.
This one was written by my teacher, Zoketsu Norman Fischer, who was actually the guiding teacher of this community for decades.
He talked about that during a session, and so it's stayed with me for a decade, more than a decade now.
The title of the poem is "Responsibility."
*Responsibility.
Tonight it's quiet, or at least the quiet is all around us.
What is it I'm worried about when I worry about anything?
What is it I tangle up in wanting to go home?
From down here I look up at myself in the little bright square of window, staring down at me in bemusement, querying what's it worth?
But that's a question snapped shut on itself, thoughts with teeth or claws to scrape away to the very core.
What cares contains its value, a half-life, mixed, no doubt, yet fair.
It's always fair, or anyway, it's always what's there, and it's not our fault, and it's not our fault.*
Norman is a man of great faith, and yet to me this poem does not read like a belief.
It reads like it is circling the same core we are pointing to in our seminar.
And then the line, "and it's not our fault," and unsaid, "and it is our responsibility," the title of the poem.
For me, that lands right next to the ancient sages who pitied them, the same movement: not excusing, not judging, just recognizing something fundamental about the human condition.
Norman approaches with elegant language that opens and softens.
Sorry, my approach is not so sophisticated.
I'm trying to find a way to let things stand plainly.
But both positions undermine a reflex, the need to secure ourselves with a conclusion.
There's a lot in that last line.
It releases something, the reflex to turn everything into self-blame or self-justification: the storm, the fear, the frozen mouse, the thoughts with teeth and claws.
None of that is a personal failure.
It is the condition of being human, not fault and responsibility.
Those two have to stay together.
If it is not our fault, we can drift into passivity.
If it's not our responsibility, then why should we care at all?
Held together, not fault and responsibility, something else appears.
We do not have to fix ourselves before we can respond.
We do not have to wait for perfect conditions before we can act.
We are already in the middle of it.
There's a line earlier in the poem: *what is it I am worried about when I worry about anything?*
One time, I was out kayaking and I thought there was a pretty good chance I wouldn't make it back to shore.
I got caught in a storm.
The weirdest thing is the only thing that floated around in my head was that question.
What is it I'm worried about when I worry about anything?
Okay, I might die.
Is that really a problem?
It's very strange how a line like that can grab you.
And in a moment of fear, that question cuts right through layers.
There is what is happening and then there is what we build on top of it, the stories we make up about possible outcomes.
Oh, I remember the other thing I was thinking of was, next stop is Hawaii.
So, some questions are not meant to be solved.

And then there is another line: *a question snaps shut on itself, teeth and claws.* We can feel how our thoughts try to grab, to secure something, to create a place where we stand where we know who we are and what we have to do and that we are permanent and this is it.
Beware of that.
That's what happens, the question snapping shut on itself.
That's what happens when you try to figure things out.
So, let's not go for intellectual analysis of this.
And by that I don't mean anti-understanding.
We're just not feeding that kind of understanding that closes other options too quickly.
So when we hear that it's not our fault and still our responsibility, it lands right here.
This is what is here and we need it.
Not as performance, not as getting it right, but as participation.
We have time for...
So, we're going to do a short triad conversation if we could just find three people together.
Each person has four minutes and you might reflect on a moment when you were outwardly still and inwardly moving or frozen.
What was it like from the inside?
Another possible question: holding the sense of not our fault and still our responsibility, does that create a shift in how you hold experience?
I'll repeat it.
One, simplified: frozen by fright.
The second one: it's not our fault and still our responsibility.
What does it feel like to you?
Thank you very much.
